newsitem.title: USA: Frost damages some N. Iowa, S. Minn corn, soy.
newsitem.headline: Frost damages some N. Iowa, S. Minn corn, soy.

text.p: Frost early Saturday morning damaged corn and soybeans in some low-lying fields in northern Iowa and southern Minnesota, agronomists said.

"The low-lying areas really got nailed," said Jurgen Peters, extension educator in Waseca County in south-central Minnesota. "North of Waseca on some of the higher, rolling ground, we had just light touches (of frost damage).
"To the south and southwest in the flat areas, some fields are fried all the way to the top six inches on the soybeans and pretty far into the corn," he added.
In northern Iowa, mature corn sustained the greatest damage, but overall damage should be minimal, said Dale Farnham, Iowa State University extension agronomist.
"In certain areas, there was some light frost damage," said Farnham. "It burned a few of the top leaves but didn't go into the canopy."

Farnham, who drove through northern Iowa on Saturday, said corn fields that had begun turning yellow sustained the most damage. Greener fields were more resistant to the cold because they respirate at night and create their own heat, he said.

Meteorologists said temperatures in low-lying areas of northern Iowa and southern Minnesota ranged from 32 to 35 degrees Fahrenheit early Saturday, but they said, in scattered areas lows may have dipped to 28 degrees.
"Chances are, there was a light freeze," said Joel Burgio, meteorologist with Weather Services Corp.
Temperatures should remain cool this week, but Burgio said forecasts do not suggest another frost in the Midwest.
However, "the pattern is volatile and subject to rapid changes," he said.

Fred Gesser, meteorologist with Weather Express Inc., said scattered rain should fall across the southern Midwest Monday and Tuesday, while high temperatures across much of the Midwest should be in the low 70s through Wednesday.
"As far as a widespread killer freeze, there is nothing in the charts to suggest that through the 25th," he said.
Waseca County's Peters said the frost occurred about 10 days early and the corn crop is about 10 days behind in development.
"You add those two together and we lost about 20 days," he said. "That may result in some light grain."
Because of the early frost, some farmers were planning to cut grain for silage this week instead of waiting for crops to dry down further, Peters said.
"We're looking at making silage like a mad fool this next week," he said. "This stuff is dead."
